extracted.intended_audience: professional copyeditors, proofreaders, authors, and publishing/production staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, editing, marking, and proofreading manuscripts and proofs for publication in print and electronic formats, including markup, change-tracking, paper markup, and production checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal markup languages and style-to-tag mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: A manuscript edited on paper or in a word processor may have to be converted and marked up ... according to the rules defined for a formal markup language such as XML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word-processing styles so styles are mapped to corresponding tags; add structural markup to delineate document hierarchy; each element identified by opening/closing tags and nested appropriately; presentation details belong in a style sheet for each publication format. Editors may need to check tags after conversion; successful workflows require significant technical expertise. Publishers may not require character-level semantic markup; for accessibility, follow WAI/W3C and EPUB Accessibility Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic tagging vs presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tagging is structural as well as semantic: each element is identified according to what it is rather than by how it is to be presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify presentation (appearance and function) separately in a style sheet; avoid using presentation-only markup for semantic elements. Note limitations of marking everything (e.g., italics) as one style for accessibility users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking changes (redlining) to show edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the change-tracking feature in word processors to produce a redlined version so authors can review edits; added text is underlined, deleted text is struck through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include author queries via commenting feature; use explanatory comments for ambiguous deletions (e.g., struck-through hyphenated term); avoid changes that might be missed—when in doubt strike out entire term and replace; be mindful of color legibility in black-and-white printouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making silent changes (not tracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to track all editing depends on factors including editor and publisher preferences; some editors track only the first instance of a global change and alert the author in a comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show trivial adjustments (e.g., margins, global smart quotes); most cleanup checklist items may be done silently. If a section was heavily edited, consider sending a clean version for author approval, and if changes were not tracked, delineate the nature of edits in a comment or cover letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using document comparison software appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Document comparison software can highlight differences between two versions automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best used with shorter documents and when comparing a cleaned latest version against an earlier cleaned version. Avoid comparing an edited document against the author's original (can produce unintelligible results). For communicating edits to authors, prefer tracked changes for predictable presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inserting comments and author queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Author queries should be inserted using the commenting feature available in most word processors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using footnotes or bracketed text to insert queries; do not add content not intended for publication into the run of text. Exceptions: structural signposts (image call-outs) or embedded notes when comments are unsupported—then place comments at the note reference marker. Include clear instructions for authors on responding to queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author review of redlined manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors reviewing changes online should be asked to use a compatible version of the software used to edit the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors cannot, provide printouts or annotated PDFs. To guard against unwanted changes, protect the manuscript with a password so author edits will be visibly tracked (but do not lose the password). Include detailed instructions for making changes and responding to queries; advise authors to use the commenting feature for replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting/rejecting tracked changes and final cleanup
rubrics_metrics.description: After the author returns the redlined manuscript the editor should go through each tracked change carefully and accept or reject it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit new material as necessary and check continuity; read author comments first to spot problems; after incorporating changes delete remaining comments and queries; run a final spelling check. Final manuscript should have no remaining tracked changes or comments except any intended for the publisher (better sent in a cover letter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a clean copy of paper manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor working on paper should always keep a clean copy of the unedited manuscript to refer to—or as a backup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If paper copy is a printout of an electronic manuscript, archiving the electronic file is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking manuscripts on paper (general rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper manuscripts are usually double-spaced so editing can appear above the word it pertains to; all editorial changes should be made in a color that will reproduce clearly if photocopied or faxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the author to respond in a color distinct from the editor's. For marking queries, write in the margin; see provided figure example for correct marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking author queries on paper manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: In manuscripts edited on paper, queries are best written in the margin; when the author has responded, they can simply be crossed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sticky notes (cannot be easily photocopied and may be detached). For extensive queries needing more space, prepare a separate keyed sheet referenced by letter or symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three uses for circling on paper manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Circling has three meanings on a manuscript: (1) circle a number/abbreviation to mean it should be spelled out; (2) circle a comma/colon to indicate a period should replace it; (3) circle a marginal comment to show it is not to be set in type but is a query or typesetting instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When circled elements could be spelled or interpreted in multiple ways, write out the required form. Circling a period already inserted prevents it from being missed when updating files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inserting, deleting, substituting on paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a regular caret (^) to indicate insertion points and an inverted caret (v) for superscripts; do not use a caret to indicate substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For substitutions cross out the deleted text and write the replacement above it so meaning is clear. Distinguish carets used for different purposes to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking added, deleted, or transposed punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to punctuation when words are transposed or deleted; punctuation must be clearly shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circle added periods, place a caret over added commas, use inverted caret under added quotation marks; if necessary write and circle the name of the punctuation (e.g., 'colon', 'exclamation point') near the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking dashes and hyphens
rubrics_metrics.description: Two hyphens with no space signal em dashes; actual em dashes, en dashes, and sequences of 2–3 em dashes should be marked; end-of-line hyphens must be marked to distinguish soft (conditional) from hard (permanent) hyphens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ambiguous, underline or cross out end-of-line hyphens to indicate whether to retain the hyphen. A global instruction may be issued (e.g., 'all hyphens between inclusive numbers are to be set as en dashes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalizing, lowercasing, and marking italics/boldface
rubrics_metrics.description: To indicate capitalization or font emphasis use conventional manuscript marks: triple underline to capitalize, double underline for small capitals, slanted line through to lowercase, straight underscore for italics, wavy underscore for boldface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works to be typeset from scratch, underlining italics usually unnecessary but may reduce missed italics; if author used both underlining and italics, provide special instructions. For mathematical copy see specialized guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking paragraph indents and vertical spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a three-sided rectangular mark to indicate moving text left or right; a symbol indicates paragraph indents; rectangular marks pointing up/down indicate vertical spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust mark width to accommodate element; to indicate a blank line write 'one-line #' and circle it ('#' signifies space). Draw a line from open side of mark to the element to be moved when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking components of a paper manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Components—chapter number/title, subheads, prose extracts, poetry—are marked with circled labels or descriptions placed at the element start or in the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handwritten labels correspond to electronic generic markup styles; circled labels (e.g., 'A' for first-level subhead) help update electronic files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading is the process of reading a text and scrutinizing all components to find errors and mark them for correction, applied after conversion to a publication format but before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreading applies to typeset/paginated proofs (paper or PDF), electronic formats other than PDF, covers/jackets, abstracts, and other published components. See proofreaders' marks and PDF markup references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are the primary proofreaders and bear final responsibility for errors; professional proofreaders may be hired by author or publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript editors, designers, and publishing personnel are responsible for ensuring corrections are incorporated and related materials are consistent and error-free. Self-publishing authors are encouraged to hire proofreaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading schedule and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreaders must be mindful that delays in returning proofs can cause major publication delays; if scheduling conflicts threaten accuracy, confer immediately with the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal proofreading deadlines are generally nonnegotiable; coordinate with production schedule references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping a record of each proofreading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A record must be kept by the publisher of when each stage of proof has been corrected and by whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For printed books maintain a master set (laser printout or PDF) with author and publisher corrections; publishers may send duplicate page proofs and transfer corrections to master set. Name PDF iterations (e.g., rev01) and collate corrections. Require sign-offs for electronic publications and packaging proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: First proofs and galley proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The author and sometimes a designated proofreader read the first proofreading copy (first proofs), usually against the edited manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex projects that may require extensive corrections, publishers might request galley proofs (loosely paginated) to avoid redoing page references in an index. The index is prepared from the first paginated proofs issued at the next stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised proofs procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: After corrections to the first proofs have been made the results must be checked for accuracy by comparing revised proofs against the first pages (foul proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for differences and introduced hyphenation or makeup problems. Do not mark on foul proofs; mark only revised printouts or PDFs. Minimize additional rounds of revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Most indexes are prepared from the paginated first set of proofs and must be proofread quickly alongside revisions to first proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors—rather than authors—usually proofread indexes; if indexes reference paragraph numbers they can be prepared from the final manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepress and press proofs checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepress proofs present an inexpensive image of what will come off the printing press and should be checked before ink is committed to paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check completeness of contents, page sequence, margins, illustration location/sizing/cropping, and spots or smudges. At press stage correct only grave errors (e.g., incorrect title or misspelled author name). Press sheets (F&Gs) may be reviewed, but corrections at this stage can require reprinting entire signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book cover and jacket proofs verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover proofs should be checked carefully; cover should be consistent with the interior in content and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure author name and title match title page; series title/volume number match interior; verify price, ISBN, and photo/artwork credit lines. Jacket and cover proofs and revisions should be reviewed by authors, editors, designers, and marketing personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal cover proofs checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Front cover (cover 1) must be checked to ensure elements that change with each issue—volume, issue number, month/date—are accurate; spine must be checked similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contents are listed on cover, check authors' names and article titles match interior and that articles are listed in correct sections. Verify inclusive page numbers on spine and check inside front/back covers for subscription or copyright info and advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading against copy (edited manuscript)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be checked against the edited manuscript (author's final changes and responses to queries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If page proofs were typeset from paper-only manuscript, read word for word against edited manuscript and ensure handwritten edits were correctly interpreted by the typesetter. Never mark the manuscript (dead/foul copy); keep it intact to assign responsibility for errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading for spelling errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreader should be alert for errors typically missed by spellcheckers, from common typos to subtle errors (it's/its, lead/led, breathe/breath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the manuscript editor's style sheet as a reference. Do not indicate global spelling changes; mark each instance and search the PDF for other appearances to evaluate consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading for word breaks and hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Check end-of-line hyphenation, especially in proper names and foreign-language terms; the first set of proofs is often the first time words are divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary for word breaks; for nondictionary words submit preferred hyphenation list to typesetter. Prefer nonstandard break if it produces better lines; avoid more than three successive lines ending in hyphens. For dividing URLs see specialized guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading for typeface and font consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that each element (chapter numbers/titles, subheads, text, extracts, figure captions) is presented in a consistent typeface and style according to the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify heads/subheads for assigned typographic style and check all set-off material for correct font/size/indentation. Ensure italics/bold start and stop as intended. Watch for conversion errors (dropped/transmuted special characters or invisible material incorporated). For systemic errors prefer a single/global instruction to avoid cluttering proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking and proofreading page numbers and running heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Page numbers and running heads must be checked to ensure correct presence and placement and that correct page number follows a blank page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm typesetter followed recto/verso instructions; running heads must be proofread and checked for placement. For endnotes verify page numbers correspond to note locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking and proofreading illustrations and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that illustrations appear in the right location, right size, orientation (not flopped), and with correct captions; check tables for content and alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure locators accurately refer to illustration parts. When a full page is occupied by illustration/table, no running head/page number should appear (unless drop folio); if several full pages occur in sequence, consider requesting page numbers or running heads to orient readers. Check lists of illustrations/tables against actual captions and page numbers; for two-page broadsides ensure facing pages.
